九州新幹線の鹿児島中央と博多の間の上下線は、電力設備の点検のため、13日始発から運転を見合わせています。【画像で見る】鹿児島中央駅などの様子　駅の窓口や高速バス乗り場に長い列運転の再開は、博多と熊本の間が13日正午ごろ、熊本と鹿児島中央の間は13日午後2時ごろを見込んでいました。しかし、JR九州によりますと、一部区間で電力設備の損傷が見つかったため、運転の再開がさらに遅れ、▼博多と熊本の間は午後4時ごろ、▼熊本と鹿児島中央の間は午後6時ごろになったということです。JR九州は、「作業の進ちょく状況によっては運転再開見込みが変わる可能性がある」としています。鹿児島中央駅では、ビジネスマンや観光客とみられる人たちが困った様子でJRの窓口を訪れていました。午前中に福岡に帰省する予定だった男性は、「運転見合わせを駅に来て初めて知った。困ったが仕方がない」と話していました。■【電力設備の損傷なにが?】JR九州によりますと、熊本市の熊本総合車両所で12日午後10時ごろ、点検中だった九州新幹線のパンタグラフから「すり板」と呼ばれる部品がなくなっているのが確認されました。ほかの車両に問題がないか確認し、およそ5時間後の13日午前3時ごろから一部の車両は徐行運転で運転を再開していました。パンタグラフや架線を含む電力設備の点検を行うため、九州新幹線は13日始発から運転を見合わせていて、午前8時半時点で上下線あわせて38本が運休となっています。■高速バス乗り場は混雑九州新幹線の運転見合わせを受け、鹿児島から熊本や福岡に向かう高速バス乗り場は、朝から混雑していました。（新幹線で博多に行く予定だった人）「こんなこと初めてです。バスターミナルに来たらちょうど1席空いていたので、無事に博多に帰れそうです」■熊本〜博多間は臨時の特急列車を運行予定JR九州は、九州新幹線の運転見合わせに伴い、熊本〜博多の在来線で、臨時特急列車の運行を予定しています。博多発　熊本行（途中停車駅:鳥栖・久留米・筑後船小屋・大牟田・玉名）熊本発　博多行（途中停車駅:鳥栖・久留米・筑後船小屋・大牟田・玉名）
臨時列車の時刻は分かり次第、ホームページなどで発表するとしています。

title: 議員会館でパーティー 文科相謝罪
body: 関芳弘文部科学相は13日の閣議後記者会見で、自身の政治資金パーティーを衆議院議員会館で開いたことを認め、「深く反省をして、もう二度とやらない」と述べた。衆院は会館内でのパーティー開催を禁止しているが、関氏は内規に抵触するとの認識がなかったという。【表で見る】26年衆院選で自民が公認した「裏金候補」43人の状況関氏側によると、2024年6月に「政経バイオフォーラム」を議員会館で開催し、81万円の収入を得た。議員会館内の食堂とすし屋などに計8万1957円を支出し、開催費用の約9割にあたる72万8043円が関氏側の利益になっていた。20年12月にも議員会館内で同様に政治資金パーティーを開催していた。衆院事務局によると、会館内での政治資金パーティーは許可されていない。関氏は「禁止行為に当たらないと個人的に判断してしまっていた」と釈明。政治資金パーティーの収入から支出を差し引いた利益は政治資金収支報告書に記載していなかったが、関氏は寄付金に当たらず記載義務はないとの認識を示した。関氏は旧安倍派。自民の派閥裏金事件で政治資金収支報告書に不記載があり処分を受けたが、簗（やな）和生農相とともに23年末の事件発覚後に初めて入閣した。【斎藤文太郎】

title: 中間選挙にマスク氏440億円投入か
body:
【ワシントン共同】米紙ニューヨーク・タイムズは12日、実業家イーロン・マスク氏が11月の中間選挙で与党共和党候補を支援するため、7月初旬以降に2億7600万ドル（約440億円）以上を投入したと伝えた。うち上院候補を支援する特別政治活動委員会（スーパーPAC）に1億5800万ドルを寄付。対抗する野党民主党系の団体が同時期に集めた献金の総額を上回り「米史上最大級の政治献金」という。【写真】「髪消された」とトランプ大統領が不満爆発　タイム誌の表紙に
対イラン作戦の長期化や物価高で共和党に逆風が吹く中、マスク氏の巨額な献金は同党に資金面で優位性をもたらしている。マスク氏には政界への影響力を確保する狙いがありそうだ。

title: 熟年離婚 修復経ず別れるケース増
body:
3組に1組が離婚する時代。実はいま、“熟年離婚”の割合が過去最高となっています。離婚カウンセラーによると、“熟年離婚”において、修復のステップを経ずに離婚へと進むケースが増えていて、「別れを切り出すのは7～8割が女性」だということです。■【動画で見る】“熟年離婚”の背景は…背景には何があるのでしょうか。“熟年離婚”の現実と対策に迫りました。
今、日本では3組に1組が離婚する時代を迎えています。9月に発表された厚生労働省の人口動態統計によると、離婚全体の件数は2002年をピークに減少傾向にあります。しかしその一方で、20年以上連れ添った夫婦が別れる“熟年離婚”の割合は過去最高の24.2％を記録しました。街頭でインタビューに応じた夫婦の多くは「大きな衝突はない」「我慢はあるけど」と苦笑いで答えます。しかし結婚18年で離婚を経験した40代女性は、「価値観が合わなくて2年前に離婚しました。24時間一緒にいたのが、段々苦痛になってきて」と当時のことを思い出し、涙をこぼしました。
35年以上にわたって離婚のカウンセリングを手がけてきた離婚カウンセラーの岡野あつこさんのもとにも、熟年離婚の相談が増えています。岡野さんが指摘する大きな特徴の一つが、離婚を切り出すのは7割から8割が女性だという点です。【離婚カウンセラー 岡野あつこさん】「離婚の準備してみようか、『修復をやってみようか』というのを飛ばすことが多くなってきました」修復のステップを経ずに離婚へと進むケースが増えていて、熟年離婚の特徴として、別れを切り出すのは7～8割が女性だということです。
熟年離婚の現実とはどのようなものなのでしょうか。大阪市内でバーを営む“まっちゃん”さん（50歳）は、去年、20年以上連れ添った妻と離婚しました。原因の1つになったのは、生活リズムのすれ違いが長年にわたって積み重なったことでした。【去年離婚した"まっちゃん"（50）】「別れる別れへんは言われずに、荷物を持って出て行って、帰ってきたら（妻が）いなかった。家がスカスカになって。いて当たり前みたいな存在だったんで、こんなことになるんやって」自宅には洗濯物が積み上げられたままに。クリーニングに出すことも後回しになり、休日には一人でご飯を食べる日々だといいます。【去年離婚した"まっちゃん"（50）】「家に帰ってきて人がいない。暗いままで帰ってくる。気持ちを察しきれていなかった後悔はある」“まっちゃん”さんのように、長年連れ添った妻と突然離婚することになった男性は、元気がなくなってしまう人が多いようです。

title: 家が買えない なぜ高騰している
body:
日本銀行は9月の金融政策決定会合で利上げを決定し、政策金利は0.25%引き上げられ、1.25%程度となった。一方で、都市部を中心にマンションや一戸建て住宅の値上がりも止まらず、家を買うハードルは年々上がっている。住宅市場でいま何が起きているのか、後悔しないためにどうすればいいのかを探った。（Yahoo!ニュース オリジナル 特集編集部／監修：山本久美子）
「建築費は1.5倍近くになり、土地の値段も高騰している大都市圏での住宅購入は高嶺の花です」不動産鑑定士の冨田建氏はこう話す。
実際に土地の価格を見てみると、京王電鉄京王線「八幡山駅」から徒歩4分の東京都杉並区の公示地「杉並-37」では、2022年には1平方メートル当たり54万6000円だったが、2026年には68万3000円に上昇。鑑定評価書では、公示地と同程度の規模で土地総額は5千万円台半ばだったのが7千万円前後と高騰している。
さらに冨田氏は不動産市場について「魅力的な労働条件を提供する企業、商業施設、文化を発信する施設等の集中する大都市圏やその周辺の郊外では住環境が良く交通利便性の優れる地域を中心に不動産価格が高い水準となっている」と説明。その一方で、「企業や商業施設、文化を発信する施設等が乏しいために労働力人口が減っている地域などの地方の不動産価格は長野県白馬村などの特殊な地域は別として下落傾向にある」として二極化が進んでいるとした。値上がりしている郊外の例として、阪神電鉄本線「鳴尾・武庫川女子大前駅」から徒歩4分に位置する兵庫県西宮市の公示地「西宮-82」は1平方メートル当たり33万1000円（22年）が40万円（26年）になった。総額は3800万円程度から4600万円へ上がり、鑑定評価書には新築の建売住宅が7千万円を超えるケースもみられると記されている。一方、函館市電湯の川線「湯の川駅」から徒歩20分で、函館の中心部から離れた北海道函館市の公示地「函館-13」では1平方メートル当たり3万7900円（22年）が、3万7600円（26年）と微減。鑑定評価書では、人口減少の影響を受け、需要が減退し地価は下落基調で推移するとみられるとしている。
冨田氏によると大都市圏やその周辺の郊外で駅に近い、店が多い、通勤しやすいといった利便性の高い場所には人が集まりやすく、不動産需要が強まるため不動産価格も高い水準になりやすい。逆に、労働力人口が減り、働く場が少ない地域や暮らすうえでの便利さが弱い地域では、不動産需要が弱く供給過多になるため、不動産価格にも値下がりの力が働くという。需要の高い場所かどうかの差が土地の値段に如実に表れているのだ。
では、家が高くなったのは土地のせいだけなのか。実は、建てる側の事情もかなり重い。
住宅ジャーナリストの山本久美子氏は、住宅高騰の背景として、資材高や人手不足などいくつもの要因が重なって、家の値段を押し上げていると分析している。
一般財団法人建設物価調査会が出している「建設物価 建築費指数®️」によると、2015年を100とした場合、2026年8月は集合住宅（鉄筋コンクリート造）で146.7、一戸建て住宅（木造）で152.7（いずれも「東京」の暫定値）を記録。約10年前と比べると同じ家を建てるのに1.5倍前後コストがかかることを意味している。
これらの要因について、山本氏はコロナ後のウッドショックやナフサ不足などによる資材の高騰や円安による輸入コストの増加が影響していると解説。また、新築住宅の省エネ基準が引き上げられ、高い断熱性能などが求められた結果、高価な資材を使う必要が出ているのだという。さらに人手不足による人件費の上昇も価格高騰に拍車をかけている。
新築マンションの建設では「土地の取り合いも過熱している」（山本氏）。駅に近く、形の整った広い土地は、マンションだけでなくホテル、オフィス、店舗にするために欲しがる。山本氏は「土地取得価格は今、新築マンションの場合は特に高くなっている」と話す。建てる前から原価が重くのしかかっているのだ。一方、新築戸建てではコロナ禍以降、在宅勤務で広さを求める動きが強まり、戸建ての需要も上向いた。高騰するマンションの受け皿として戸建て物件を探す人が増えた面もあり、価格は上昇している。
中古市場はどうだろうか。山本氏は、「新築と比べてこの価格なら割安だねといって買ってくれる」傾向があるとして、需要と供給のバランスで変わってくると指摘。新築物件の価格高騰に伴い上昇傾向にあるのに加え、リフォーム物件では資材高騰の影響を受け、価格がさらに上昇しているとした。
住みやすい場所では土地価格も建築費も上がる。住宅が買いにくくなっているところに追い打ちをかけるのが金利負担の上昇だ。
日銀は2024年3月にマイナス金利を解除して以降、段階的に利上げを実施。今年6月と9月にも政策金利を0.25%引き上げ、現在の政策金利は1.25%程度。日銀は今後も政策金利の引き上げを行うとみられる。
金利の引き上げは家計にどのような影響を与えるだろうか。借入額と年収別に返済負担率を見てみよう。
より詳しく自分の返済負担率を知りたい場合は、以下のシミュレーターから計算してみてください。借入条件と世帯年収を入力すると、返済額と返済負担率の目安を試算できます。
では、この数字をどう受け止めればいいのか。山本氏に、返済負担率の見方や金利の選び方を聞いた。
住宅の価格も金利も上がり続けるなか、「人生で一番高い買い物」を後悔なくするにはどうしたらいいだろうか。
「住宅を購入して後悔する典型例は誰かに言われて家を選ぶ人です。買い時は外的要因に求めないで、自分のタイミング、内的要因で決めたほうがいい」
山本氏は住宅購入の最適なタイミングについて、「今、買いたいという要因が明確ならそのときが住宅購入のベストなタイミング」と断言。市場の動向（価格や金利）や他人の勧めといった外的要因ではなく、子育てや働き方の変化、趣味のための空間確保といった住宅購入の動機がはっきりしているときに買うと後悔が減るとしている。
さらに、「変えられないものに不満をもったらどうしようもない」として、広さや建物の構造、立地といった後から変えられないものの優先順位を上げて検討すると住んだ後の後悔が減るという。比較検討も重要だ。マンションの場合、同じような間取りや仕様になることが多い。そこで、1つだけ見て決めるよりも複数の物件を見て、本当に必要なものは何か考え、目を養うことが理想の家に出会うコツだ。
冨田氏にも山本氏にも共通している見解がある。それは、住宅が高騰している要因が解消される見込みはなく、住宅価格がすぐに安くなることはないということだ。そんななか、上手に家を買うためには、選択肢を広げること。新築を中古に変える。都心のマンションに固執せず郊外の戸建ても見る。急行停車駅ではなく各駅停車駅を選ぶ。駅徒歩5分以内ではなく、10分前後まで許容する。家を選ぶ条件の中で何を残し、何を緩めるかで選択肢は大きく変わる。
山本氏は「市況が改善するタイミングを待つよりは家を買いたいタイミングに合わせて選択肢を広げて考えていくほうがその人にとっていいと思います」とアドバイス。「そのために、まず目安でもいいので予算を決める。そこから予算内で条件に合う範囲で選ぶというスタンスがいいでしょう」と語った。
「#生活危機」は、Yahoo!ニュースがユーザーと考えたい社会課題「ホットイシュー」の一つです。物価高、不安定な雇用、社会保険料や税金の増加。お金や生活をめぐる諸問題のために、私たちができることは何か。対策や解説などの情報を発信しています。

title: ICC制裁 赤根智子所長がコメント
body:
アメリカのトランプ政権がＩＣＣ（国際刑事裁判所）を制裁対象に指定したことを受け、赤根智子所長がＡＢＣテレビの取材に対し、日本を含む締約国に協力を呼びかけるとともに、国内から支援が寄せられていることへの感謝を述べました。【大阪都構想】４つの特別区の名称めぐる「最終アンケート」開始　２７日までアメリカは９日、ＩＣＣの元判事がノーベル平和賞に決まった直後、ＩＣＣへの制裁を発表しました。これを踏まえ、赤根所長は１２日までに、ＡＢＣテレビの取材にコメントを寄せました。「ＩＣＣの理念に賛同し、これを支えてきた日本を含む締約国は、ＩＣＣを守るために今こそ連帯を確認し、ともに立ち上がらねばなりません。ＩＣＣが独立した裁判所として活動し続けられるために必要かつ具体的な手段をもって支えてもらえると信じています」と協力を呼びかけました。その上で、「私はそのために最善を尽くします」と述べ、活動を継続していく決意を改めて表明し、「日本の皆様の応援と温かい言葉の数々が私を勇気づけてくれています」と日本で広がる支援に対し感謝を述べました。また、日本への期待も示しました。「日本人は、法の支配による正義の実現の大切さを知っています。法による正義は、それとは対極にあるものに打ち勝たねばならないと思って、支えてくれる。とてもありがたいです。特に、次の世代の人達、若い世代には奮起と行動を期待しています」一方、戦争犯罪の被害者や家族への支援や賠償を行う「ＩＣＣ被害者信託基金」に、日本から多くの支援金が寄せられていることも明かし、「とても感謝しています」と言葉にしました。
さらに、日本には国外で起きたジェノサイドや外国人同士の戦争犯罪などを裁くことを目的とした国内法がないと指摘し、その必要性を訴えました。「そうした犯罪者がたまたま日本に来て、そうした犯罪を犯した人だとわかっても、日本の捜査機関や裁判所は手出しができず、締約国であっても、ローマ規程による補完性の原則に従うことができないのです。では、ＩＣＣに引き渡せばよいのでは？という人もいるかもしれませんが、日本では何らの犯罪も犯していない人、処罰できない人を日本はどうするか考えてみます。ＩＣＣがその人に逮捕状を出して、日本に引き渡せと言ってくる場合は良いでしょう。そういう場合は日本は、ＩＣＣからの逮捕状やそれについての必要な証拠などを渡されますから、日本の裁判所の判断で引き渡すことも可能になります。しかし、ＩＣＣはいわゆる犯罪の中心人物、「大物」を中心に捜査をし、逮捕状を出しますから、日本にいるその人にＩＣＣの逮捕状が出ている場合は限定的（小物なら出ていない可能性大）です。ＩＣＣの逮捕状が出ていない場合には日本が勝手にＩＣＣに身柄を送るわけにもいかず、自らの判断で裁判するしかないはずですが、日本に国内法がないとそれもできないということになります。また、その犯罪を犯した人の本国がその人を国に返せと言ってきた場合に日本の当局はどのようにするでしょうか。実際、ＩＣＣにある戦争犯罪などを国内法化した多くのＩＣＣ締約国では、そうした事件を自分の国で裁いています。それはＩＣＣを間接的に助け、世界における『不処罰を無くす』ための努力にも加わっているのです。日本はそうした世界の国々の努力に参加できていないのです」（全文掲載）

title: 中間選挙にマスク氏440億円投入か
body:
【ワシントン共同】米紙ニューヨーク・タイムズは12日、実業家イーロン・マスク氏が11月の中間選挙で与党共和党候補を支援するため、7月初旬以降に2億7600万ドル（約440億円）以上を投入したと伝えた。うち上院候補を支援する特別政治活動委員会（スーパーPAC）に1億5800万ドルを寄付。対抗する野党民主党系の団体が同時期に集めた献金の総額を上回り「米史上最大級の政治献金」という。【写真】「髪消された」とトランプ大統領が不満爆発　タイム誌の表紙に
対イラン作戦の長期化や物価高で共和党に逆風が吹く中、マスク氏の巨額な献金は同党に資金面で優位性をもたらしている。マスク氏には政界への影響力を確保する狙いがありそうだ。

title: 平和賞のピレイ氏 ICC職員を激励
body: 今年のノーベル平和賞受賞が決まったインド系南アフリカ人の法律家ナビ・ピレイ氏（85）が12日、かつて裁判官として働いたオランダ・ハーグの国際刑事裁判所（ICC）を訪れた。報道機関には公開されなかったが、ICCによると、米国による制裁決定で存亡の危機にあるICCの職員を激励した。【動画】赤根所長「力こそ正義の世界選ぶのか」ICCによると、ピレイ氏は赤根智子所長ら職員900人以上を前に、困難な時代にICCが果たす重要な役割に敬意を表し、活動に携わる人びとの献身をたたえた。「皆さんの思いやりと勇気が、不処罰をはびこらせないための力となり続けている」と述べたという。赤根氏はピレイ氏の受賞決定を祝福し、「恒久平和の礎として国際司法が果たす非常に重要な役割が認められた」と強調。訪問は1時間ほどで終了したという。

title: 正恩氏と「会うかも」トランプ氏
body:
【ワシントン共同】トランプ米大統領は12日、来月に予定するアジア訪問に合わせて北朝鮮の金正恩朝鮮労働党総書記と「会うかもしれない」と述べた。ホワイトハウスで記者団に語った。これまでも金氏との会談実現に意欲を示してきた。【写真】「髪消された」とトランプ大統領が不満爆発　タイム誌の表紙に
トランプ氏は11月に中国広東省深センで開かれるアジア太平洋経済協力会議（APEC）首脳会議に出席する予定。香港紙によると、同月にフィリピンで開かれる東南アジア諸国連合（ASEAN）首脳会議にも出席する方向で調整している。トランプ氏は北朝鮮の核保有を公然と認めるような発言を繰り返してきた。核保有国認定を求める北朝鮮側に秋波を送っているとの見方もある。

title: 英基地事件はイラン関与 共同声明
body: アメリカ軍も駐留するイギリス空軍基地近くで、テロを準備した疑いで7人の男が逮捕された事件で、イギリスやアメリカなど29か国の外相は「イランの関与をイギリスが特定したことを認める」とする共同声明を発表しました。【写真で見る】テロ準備か 英国空軍基地近くで5人逮捕イギリスのフェアフォード空軍基地近くで先月27日未明、テロを準備したとしてイギリス国籍の男5人が逮捕された事件では、その後、イギリスとイランの二重国籍を持つ男なども逮捕され、これまでに合わせて7人が逮捕されています。これについて12日、イギリスやアメリカなど29か国の外相は「フェアフォード空軍基地とイランの国家脅威に関する共同声明」を発表しました。声明は、フェアフォード空軍基地の事件について「イランの関与をイギリスが特定したことを認める」としたほか、「秘密裏に構築されたネットワークや代理勢力を通じ、国境を越えて敵対的な活動を展開しようとするイラン革命防衛隊の継続的な意欲を示すものであると断定した」と主張しています。また、イランに対し「人々を脅迫したり、沈黙させたり、危害を加えたりするなどのいかなる試みも容認できない」と警告しています。

title: 九州新幹線 運転再開は夕方以降に
body:
九州新幹線の鹿児島中央と博多の間の上下線は、電力設備の点検のため、13日始発から運転を見合わせています。【画像で見る】鹿児島中央駅などの様子　駅の窓口や高速バス乗り場に長い列運転の再開は、博多と熊本の間が13日正午ごろ、熊本と鹿児島中央の間は13日午後2時ごろを見込んでいました。しかし、JR九州によりますと、一部区間で電力設備の損傷が見つかったため、運転の再開がさらに遅れ、▼博多と熊本の間は午後4時ごろ、▼熊本と鹿児島中央の間は午後6時ごろになったということです。JR九州は、「作業の進ちょく状況によっては運転再開見込みが変わる可能性がある」としています。鹿児島中央駅では、ビジネスマンや観光客とみられる人たちが困った様子でJRの窓口を訪れていました。午前中に福岡に帰省する予定だった男性は、「運転見合わせを駅に来て初めて知った。困ったが仕方がない」と話していました。■【電力設備の損傷なにが?】JR九州によりますと、熊本市の熊本総合車両所で12日午後10時ごろ、点検中だった九州新幹線のパンタグラフから「すり板」と呼ばれる部品がなくなっているのが確認されました。ほかの車両に問題がないか確認し、およそ5時間後の13日午前3時ごろから一部の車両は徐行運転で運転を再開していました。パンタグラフや架線を含む電力設備の点検を行うため、九州新幹線は13日始発から運転を見合わせていて、午前8時半時点で上下線あわせて38本が運休となっています。■高速バス乗り場は混雑九州新幹線の運転見合わせを受け、鹿児島から熊本や福岡に向かう高速バス乗り場は、朝から混雑していました。（新幹線で博多に行く予定だった人）「こんなこと初めてです。バスターミナルに来たらちょうど1席空いていたので、無事に博多に帰れそうです」■熊本〜博多間は臨時の特急列車を運行予定JR九州は、九州新幹線の運転見合わせに伴い、熊本〜博多の在来線で、臨時特急列車の運行を予定しています。博多発　熊本行（途中停車駅:鳥栖・久留米・筑後船小屋・大牟田・玉名）熊本発　博多行（途中停車駅:鳥栖・久留米・筑後船小屋・大牟田・玉名）
臨時列車の時刻は分かり次第、ホームページなどで発表するとしています。

title: ノーベル経済学賞 米大教授2人に
body: ［ストックホルム　１２日　ロイター］ - スウェーデン王立科学アカデミーは１２日、２０２６年のノーベル経済学賞を米スタンフォード大学のロバート・ホール‌教授（８３）と米コロンビア大学のマイケル・ウッドフォード教授（７０）⁠に授与すると発表した。授賞理由は「マクロ経済の安定化に関するミクロ経済学的基盤」。両氏は、効果的な安定化政策を実行する能力を​向上させる新たなボトムアップ型の経済モデルを開発した。これにより、経済に打撃を与える変動の激しさを緩和で‌きる、適切なタイミングでの財政・金融政策の実施が可能となり、世界の中央銀行や財務省で活用されている。経済学賞選考委員会のジョン・‌ハスラー委員長は声明で「両氏‌の功績は、現在世界中の各中央銀行や政府によっ​て使われているモデルに安定した理論的基盤を提供した」と指摘。「両氏のモデルに‌よって、エネルギー危機や家計消費の急変動など、経済へのショックにより適切に対処できるようにな‌った」と述べた。両氏の重要な​洞察の一つは、経済の仕組みを上から捉えるトップダウン‌型の理論に頼るのではなく、家計や企業がミクロのレベルで下す無数の決定を考慮し⁠て初めて経済を安定させられるという点だ。ウッドフォード氏は会見で「当局は、経済の安定化を、経済の中にいる人々がそれをどう理解しているかとは関係なく、誰かがレバー⁠を引いて経済を操作するだけの作業と見なすべきでは​ない」と語った。ウッドフ‌ォード氏によると、中銀が高騰するインフレへの対応に苦しんだ１９７０年代の石油危機とは違い、２０００年代後半の世界金融危機では、新たな枠組みが伝統的な金融政策手段⁠を補う上で役に立った。「すぐに追加利下げできることだけに頼る⁠のではなく、金利政策が今後どうなりそうかをより明確に表明することが、０９年以降の政策対応⁠の重要な部分を占めた」と述べた。両氏の研究は、金融政策の先行きを示す、いわゆる「フォ‌ワードガ⁠イダンス」のほかにも、需要が変化しても価格の変化が遅れる「粘​着的な」インフレ、「需給ギャップ（アウトプットギャップ）」といった現在使われている概念を広めた。

title: 家が買えない なぜ高騰している
body:
日本銀行は9月の金融政策決定会合で利上げを決定し、政策金利は0.25%引き上げられ、1.25%程度となった。一方で、都市部を中心にマンションや一戸建て住宅の値上がりも止まらず、家を買うハードルは年々上がっている。住宅市場でいま何が起きているのか、後悔しないためにどうすればいいのかを探った。（Yahoo!ニュース オリジナル 特集編集部／監修：山本久美子）
「建築費は1.5倍近くになり、土地の値段も高騰している大都市圏での住宅購入は高嶺の花です」不動産鑑定士の冨田建氏はこう話す。
実際に土地の価格を見てみると、京王電鉄京王線「八幡山駅」から徒歩4分の東京都杉並区の公示地「杉並-37」では、2022年には1平方メートル当たり54万6000円だったが、2026年には68万3000円に上昇。鑑定評価書では、公示地と同程度の規模で土地総額は5千万円台半ばだったのが7千万円前後と高騰している。
さらに冨田氏は不動産市場について「魅力的な労働条件を提供する企業、商業施設、文化を発信する施設等の集中する大都市圏やその周辺の郊外では住環境が良く交通利便性の優れる地域を中心に不動産価格が高い水準となっている」と説明。その一方で、「企業や商業施設、文化を発信する施設等が乏しいために労働力人口が減っている地域などの地方の不動産価格は長野県白馬村などの特殊な地域は別として下落傾向にある」として二極化が進んでいるとした。値上がりしている郊外の例として、阪神電鉄本線「鳴尾・武庫川女子大前駅」から徒歩4分に位置する兵庫県西宮市の公示地「西宮-82」は1平方メートル当たり33万1000円（22年）が40万円（26年）になった。総額は3800万円程度から4600万円へ上がり、鑑定評価書には新築の建売住宅が7千万円を超えるケースもみられると記されている。一方、函館市電湯の川線「湯の川駅」から徒歩20分で、函館の中心部から離れた北海道函館市の公示地「函館-13」では1平方メートル当たり3万7900円（22年）が、3万7600円（26年）と微減。鑑定評価書では、人口減少の影響を受け、需要が減退し地価は下落基調で推移するとみられるとしている。
冨田氏によると大都市圏やその周辺の郊外で駅に近い、店が多い、通勤しやすいといった利便性の高い場所には人が集まりやすく、不動産需要が強まるため不動産価格も高い水準になりやすい。逆に、労働力人口が減り、働く場が少ない地域や暮らすうえでの便利さが弱い地域では、不動産需要が弱く供給過多になるため、不動産価格にも値下がりの力が働くという。需要の高い場所かどうかの差が土地の値段に如実に表れているのだ。
では、家が高くなったのは土地のせいだけなのか。実は、建てる側の事情もかなり重い。
住宅ジャーナリストの山本久美子氏は、住宅高騰の背景として、資材高や人手不足などいくつもの要因が重なって、家の値段を押し上げていると分析している。
一般財団法人建設物価調査会が出している「建設物価 建築費指数®️」によると、2015年を100とした場合、2026年8月は集合住宅（鉄筋コンクリート造）で146.7、一戸建て住宅（木造）で152.7（いずれも「東京」の暫定値）を記録。約10年前と比べると同じ家を建てるのに1.5倍前後コストがかかることを意味している。
これらの要因について、山本氏はコロナ後のウッドショックやナフサ不足などによる資材の高騰や円安による輸入コストの増加が影響していると解説。また、新築住宅の省エネ基準が引き上げられ、高い断熱性能などが求められた結果、高価な資材を使う必要が出ているのだという。さらに人手不足による人件費の上昇も価格高騰に拍車をかけている。
新築マンションの建設では「土地の取り合いも過熱している」（山本氏）。駅に近く、形の整った広い土地は、マンションだけでなくホテル、オフィス、店舗にするために欲しがる。山本氏は「土地取得価格は今、新築マンションの場合は特に高くなっている」と話す。建てる前から原価が重くのしかかっているのだ。一方、新築戸建てではコロナ禍以降、在宅勤務で広さを求める動きが強まり、戸建ての需要も上向いた。高騰するマンションの受け皿として戸建て物件を探す人が増えた面もあり、価格は上昇している。
中古市場はどうだろうか。山本氏は、「新築と比べてこの価格なら割安だねといって買ってくれる」傾向があるとして、需要と供給のバランスで変わってくると指摘。新築物件の価格高騰に伴い上昇傾向にあるのに加え、リフォーム物件では資材高騰の影響を受け、価格がさらに上昇しているとした。
住みやすい場所では土地価格も建築費も上がる。住宅が買いにくくなっているところに追い打ちをかけるのが金利負担の上昇だ。
日銀は2024年3月にマイナス金利を解除して以降、段階的に利上げを実施。今年6月と9月にも政策金利を0.25%引き上げ、現在の政策金利は1.25%程度。日銀は今後も政策金利の引き上げを行うとみられる。
金利の引き上げは家計にどのような影響を与えるだろうか。借入額と年収別に返済負担率を見てみよう。
より詳しく自分の返済負担率を知りたい場合は、以下のシミュレーターから計算してみてください。借入条件と世帯年収を入力すると、返済額と返済負担率の目安を試算できます。
では、この数字をどう受け止めればいいのか。山本氏に、返済負担率の見方や金利の選び方を聞いた。
住宅の価格も金利も上がり続けるなか、「人生で一番高い買い物」を後悔なくするにはどうしたらいいだろうか。
「住宅を購入して後悔する典型例は誰かに言われて家を選ぶ人です。買い時は外的要因に求めないで、自分のタイミング、内的要因で決めたほうがいい」
山本氏は住宅購入の最適なタイミングについて、「今、買いたいという要因が明確ならそのときが住宅購入のベストなタイミング」と断言。市場の動向（価格や金利）や他人の勧めといった外的要因ではなく、子育てや働き方の変化、趣味のための空間確保といった住宅購入の動機がはっきりしているときに買うと後悔が減るとしている。
さらに、「変えられないものに不満をもったらどうしようもない」として、広さや建物の構造、立地といった後から変えられないものの優先順位を上げて検討すると住んだ後の後悔が減るという。比較検討も重要だ。マンションの場合、同じような間取りや仕様になることが多い。そこで、1つだけ見て決めるよりも複数の物件を見て、本当に必要なものは何か考え、目を養うことが理想の家に出会うコツだ。
冨田氏にも山本氏にも共通している見解がある。それは、住宅が高騰している要因が解消される見込みはなく、住宅価格がすぐに安くなることはないということだ。そんななか、上手に家を買うためには、選択肢を広げること。新築を中古に変える。都心のマンションに固執せず郊外の戸建ても見る。急行停車駅ではなく各駅停車駅を選ぶ。駅徒歩5分以内ではなく、10分前後まで許容する。家を選ぶ条件の中で何を残し、何を緩めるかで選択肢は大きく変わる。
山本氏は「市況が改善するタイミングを待つよりは家を買いたいタイミングに合わせて選択肢を広げて考えていくほうがその人にとっていいと思います」とアドバイス。「そのために、まず目安でもいいので予算を決める。そこから予算内で条件に合う範囲で選ぶというスタンスがいいでしょう」と語った。
「#生活危機」は、Yahoo!ニュースがユーザーと考えたい社会課題「ホットイシュー」の一つです。物価高、不安定な雇用、社会保険料や税金の増加。お金や生活をめぐる諸問題のために、私たちができることは何か。対策や解説などの情報を発信しています。

title: マンション高騰 売れ残り値下げも
body: 高騰しているマンション価格に変化の兆しです。東京・港区の部屋は2000万円の値下げに。その理由は。【動画】マンション価格「ワニの口」現象　売買成立せず在庫が急増　売り手も買い手も苦境■衝撃…「2000万円値下げ」も東京・港区の中古マンション。クラフトレジデンス　山口剛平社長「山手線の駅から9分前後」JR山手線の田町駅から徒歩10分圏内の好立地です。専有部分の面積は約70平米。ウォークインクローゼットにつながる8畳の部屋と5畳の部屋がある2LDK。しかも、築年数がまだ10年も経っていないうえに…。クラフトレジデンス　山口剛平社長「食洗器とコンロを新品に交換している」壁紙や水回りを中心にリノベーションも施されています。にもかかわらず最近、販売価格を大幅に引き下げたといいます。クラフトレジデンス　山口剛平社長「2000万円下がっている。1億5990万円まで値引き」相場を見ながら売主と相談して決めるという販売価格。当初、5月に1億7990万円で売り出された部屋は、その後1000万円値下げ。さらに最近、追加で1000万円価格を下げることに。なぜ値下げしたのでしょうか。クラフトレジデンス　山口剛平社長「売れ残っている。足踏みしている」背景の一つとみられるのが“金利のある世界”の到来です。クラフトレジデンス　山口剛平社長「極端に金利が上がって様子見しているような状態」長期金利は3％超えで推移していて、「フラット35」の適用金利は過去最高の更新が続く状況で、今月の最低金利は先月の3.46％から3.83％に引き上げられました。このひと月分の金利上昇分だけでも試算してもらうと…。住宅ローンに詳しい住宅ジャーナリスト　山本久美子さん「1億6000万円くらいのものを例えば自己資金を3割入れて1億1200万円をフラット35で借りたとすると、2万5000円弱の金額が毎月負担が増える形に」将来的に1000万円を超えるような負担増。これが一時的に様子見の人を増やしているのは間違いなさそうです。このままマンションの価格は下がるのでしょうか。住宅ジャーナリスト　山本久美子さん「マンションの価格が下がるよりも前に“金利は上がっていくだろう”。『価格が下がるのを待つ』と金利が上がって、より買いづらくなる。必ずしも金利が上がって買い手が減って（価格が）下がるとは言い切れない」

title: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
summary: Despite the US president announcing energy infrastructure would not be targeted strikes have continued, Ukraine says.
body:
Emergency services responded to a Russian drone strike on a residential building in Kharkiv, north-eastern Ukraine on Monday
Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities".
There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
Zelensky backs Trump's 'energy ceasefire' but says Russia continues to hit power plants
Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.
He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities."
"I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added.
Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan toimport Russian diesel into the USon Friday.
On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported"new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.
Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said.
Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire".
On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district.
Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured.
Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire claim mean for Ukraine?
When Trump firstannounced the ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire".
Asked about the ceasefire on Monday, Trump said they agreed "because I said you agree", adding that the war "has to get settled".
"That war is a disaster if you see the numbers," he said.
For months, Ukraine and Russia have beenexchanging strikes on energy infrastructure, disrupting energy supplies on both sides.
Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".
Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter.
In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025.
Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year.
Energy facilities in Kharkiv were hit by Russian strikes on Sunday evening, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said
Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.
The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.
However, there has been a mixed response among European officials.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."
Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working".
Additional reporting by Benedict Garman, BBC Verify

title: Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire
summary: While Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggests he would sign up to a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, Russia has said little.
body:
Employees of DTEK energy company in Ukraine work to restore power supply following a missile strike in July
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure "effective immediately". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggested it was "news for me", while Russia has not commented publicly.
So who is saying what?
Donald Trump says an energy ceasefire has been agreed.
Kyiv asks: Has it? It is willing to sign up – if Russia does.
Russia is saying: Very little.
Russian President Vladimir Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked whether such a ceasefire had been agreed during his daily conference call with journalists.
"Contacts are continuing," Peskov replied.
"As soon as we have anything to say about this, we will definitely inform you."
Peskov may not have had much to say on the matter, but the pro-Kremlin media has.
It has dubbed President Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire "a gift" for Moscow.
"Of course we benefit," pro-government news outlet Moskovsky Komsomolets concluded.
"It means that all Russia has to do is not destroy Ukraine's last remaining oil refinery.
"That has already been attacked several times. It's barely functioning anyway.
"But Kyiv won't be allowed to hit the multitude of refineries we have.
"In effect it's a one-way deal that benefits us. That's why no one here has officially rejected it."
In other words, Moscow believes Trump's announcement ties Ukraine's hands, not Russia's.
In recent months, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities have caused extensive damage, as well as fuel shortages across the country.
Should such attacks continue, expect the Russians to claim that Kyiv is harming US economic interests – as well as the Republican Party's chances in the midterm elections in November.
Russian officials will argue that the strikes underminethe recent Trump-Putin fuel deal for the US to import Russian diesel.
Trump has claimed the agreement will benefit US consumers, although there is widespread scepticism that the volumes involved will do much to lower fuel prices.
Vladimir Putin has shown little desire to stop the fighting
Still, the Kremlin will be only too happy if Ukrainian drone strikes on oil facilities spark fury in the White House and curtail US support for Kyiv.
Moscow would welcome Washington cutting off intelligence sharing to Ukraine and weapons sales to Europe that are destined for Kyiv.
It has already delighted to hear Trump declaring: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called for a 60-day Russian ceasefire to allow for presidential elections in Ukraine.
"The Kremlin, the president, has said many times before, we don't want a ceasefire, we want a lasting peace, and we're willing to do whatever's possible for that," Peskov said.
"Whatever's possible" does not include a 60-day ceasefire, or a 30-day ceasefire, or anything close to that.
On Monday, the Kremlin proposed a one-day cessation of hostilities for Ukraine to hold elections.
That will not be seen in Ukraine, or in the West, as a serious offer.
It comes as no surprise though.
Putin has shown little desire to halt the fighting.
Recent statements, speeches and signals from Russia's leader suggest that, with winter approaching, the Kremlin is counting on a continued campaign of Russian strikes to significantly increase the pressure on Ukraine.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
The Kremlin has claimed to seek "lasting peace" but right now it is continuing the fighting.
On Monday, Zelensky claimed that Russia had hit several energy targets across Ukraine during the night and into the morning.
"This window of opportunity should be used to knock Ukraine back to the Stone Age and force it to accept peace on Russia's terms," the pro-government Moskovsky Komsomolets has written.
The Kremlin's objective hasn't changed: Ukraine's capitulation.
Moscow seems to believe that the diesel deal with Trump and the US president's growing impatience with Zelensky will help Russia secure its goal.

title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth, BBC finds
summary: Backdated paperwork also made the Russian oligarch’s yachts and mansions disappear from accounts, investigation finds.
body:
Watch: The documents that were falsified to allow Roman Abramovich to evade tax
The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.
Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.
Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".
Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".
The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.
For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.
Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.
The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".
Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.
Chateau de la Croe (top left) in the south of France, Fyning Hill in Sussex and two superyachts vanished from company accounts
The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022.
The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well asthe Bureau of Investigative Journalism,external- have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of theInternational Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential,externalinvestigation.
In 2022, Panorama also reported on howAbramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt dealto buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false.
The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city.
Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune.
The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices.
Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune
He was the Russian oligarch who brought his wealth to the UK. But what’s the truth about Roman Abramovich’s fortune? Panorama investigates the documents that were falsified to hide his wealth and evade tax.
Watch now on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 12 October.
Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth.
Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property.
A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus.
Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax
To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history. They drew up a plan to circumvent the transparency law by transferring the assets to Amiscan's parent company in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), where they could be kept hidden. And they backdated  the change by three years to make it look like the asset transfer had happened in 2003.
Deloitte Cyprus reviewed the backdated documents and said they were "adequate" to allow them to remove the assets from Amiscan's accounts.
When the 2003 accounts were signed off by Deloitte in 2006, the homes, planes and yachts disappeared at the stroke of a pen. Only $75,000 of assets remained.
Deloitte signed off the accounts even though the leaked documents show it knew they were completely misleading.
Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.
Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.
This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.
It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.
But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history.
Abramovich's close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest
An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read.
MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money.
A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree".
MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI.
This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus.
Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets.
So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax.
Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said.
Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law."
In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus.
MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune.
It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public.
Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier.
MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000.
Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear.
Andrew Mitchell KC told Panorama: "What you take away from it is there are professionals who are prepared to bend and break the rules of their profession and therefore the law. And it looks that they will stop literally at nothing in terms of creating documents."
Vladimir Milov, Russia's deputy minister of energy as Abramovich built his empire and now a critic of the Russian government, said: "For each Russian oligarch or Middle Eastern or African corrupt oligarch, there's an army of Western financial and legal services and PR services providers, who is easily taking money for whitewashing their reputation and making them look normal."
Denying any wrongdoing by the oligarch, Roman Abramovich's lawyers said that he was "not involved in the day-to-day operation of those companies" and that where arrangements were proposed by professional advisers, "reliance on that advice was entirely proper and legitimate".

title: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
summary: It comes after the armed group hit Riyadh's international airport and another facility, killing 13 people, in a significant escalation.
body:
Watch: Footage from inside Riyadh's airport shows the moment the strike hit on Saturday
Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement.
"The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.
On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure.
The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.
The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.
A Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.
Explosions were heard again in Riyadh on Monday night, with the Saudi-led military coalition saying a ballistic missile had been intercepted and destroyed.
A Houthi spokesperson said the group had again targeted the airport.
Meanwhile, Qatar Airways has said it will temporarily suspend flights to Riyadh and the north-eastern city of Dammam.
Etihad Airways said it had cancelled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to "regional disruption".
King Khalid airport is expected to remain closed until Saturday.
The WPC Energy Congress opened on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km (6 miles) from Riyadh's airport, which has been attacked four times over the past week.
Last Thursday, three Saudis, including a pilot for the national airline Saudia, were killed in two strikes on an airport facility and an aircraft on the ground.
Another four Saudis, as well as two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, one Sudanese and one Indian, were killed in Saturday's missile strike on Terminal 3.
On Sunday, a Pakistani resident was killed when a projectile hit Terminal 4, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was also attacked on Sunday evening, it said, but no casualties were reported.
Later, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces had intercepted a drone in Eastern Province and a missile launched by the Houthis towards the south-western city of Khamis Mushait.
In his inaugural address to the WPC Energy Congress on Monday, Prince Abdul Aziz thanked industry executives and policymakers for attending despite the attacks.
"You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart," he said.
But he also acknowledged that "energy security cannot be taken for granted" and that recent developments had "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience".
Prince Abdul Aziz promised that his country would overcome those challenges.
"We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people," he said. "We shall prove it to the world that whatever we are going through we will overcome it."
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
Sarea also reiterated a warning to airlines and passengers against using Saudi airports and airspace, except for journeys to and from the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis' forces, he vowed, would "continue their escalating operations deep inside Saudi, imposing the equation of 'a blockade for a blockade' and 'an escalation for an escalation' and targeting Saudi enemy reinforcements until the aggression ceases and the siege on our dear people is lifted".
Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport drew widespread international condemnation.
UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" and warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure were a violation of international law.
President Donald Trump said he would "make a decision" about the US joining Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis. The US military is reportedly already providing intelligence and targeting support to the Saudi-led coalition.
Iran, which has repeatedly denied allegations that it provides weapons and training to the Houthis, said it was "deeply concerned" by the escalation and called for "dialogue and engagement" to resolve the situation.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.
Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

title: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies aged 34
summary: Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, starred as Walter White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series.
body:
Watch: "It's nice to see everyone", says RJ Mitte at Breaking Bad reunion
US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series Breaking Bad, has died aged 34.
"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," his representative told the BBC.
He died in Brownsville, Texas. No immediate cause of death was provided.
Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, drew on his own experience for his role as Walter White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series starring Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul. He earned a Screen Actors Guild Award in 2014 for his work on the series.
"Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," his representative, Sean Reilly, said in a statement to the BBC.
Mitte also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's.
He created The Mitte Foundation as well, to support philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, using his platform "to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities", Reilly said.
The Brownsville Police Department confirmed the actor's passing in a statement to the BBC, saying the cause and manner of death have not been determined and the investigation remains ongoing. No foul play was suspected, according to police.
The actor was declared dead on 12 October at what was believed to be his home, Cameron County Justice of the Peace, Cyndi Hinojosa, told the Associated Press, adding that a post-mortem examination would be performed.
Breaking Bad aired on US cable broadcaster AMC for five seasons from 2008-13.
The anti-hero drama created by Vince Gilligan earned a whopping 58 Primetime Emmy nominations and won 16, including two for Outstanding Drama Series in 2013 and 2014.
Cranston plays a high school chemistry teacher in New Mexico who turns to a life of crime to support his family after a cancer diagnosis. As he descends deeper into the underbelly of the meth trade, he drifts further from his son, Walt Jr, who makes his displeasure known with levity through much of the series.
In a statement shared with the Hollywood Reporter, Aaron Paul, who played one of the show's lead characters, Jesse Pinkman, said he was at a loss and heartbroken.
"RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed," he said. "And to whoever happens to be reading this, please know you are loved, and you are not alone. Always remember that."
Dean Norris, who played Mitte's uncle, Hank Schrader, posted that although "RJ didn't play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set".
"He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed," Norris wrote.
The Breaking Bad cast at the SAG Awards in 2014
Mitte, who grew up in Louisiana, was a young teen when he auditioned for the breakthrough role after moving to Los Angeles to support his younger sister's acting career in 2005.
He had said that his first audition in Los Angeles was for a California state public service announcement for an anti-meth commercial.
"Fast forward to auditioning for Breaking Bad, which is still, in my opinion, an anti-meth thing because it doesn't end well for anyone," he said on the Joe Vulpis Podcast earlier this month.
His character was based on Gilligan's late friend who had a more severe case of cerebral palsy and used forearm crutches, which Mitte did not require.
Mitte was seen as playing the role with honesty and accessibility, cracking jokes as a teen whose health condition was never mentioned in the series.
After shooting to fame, Mitte fought for more varied roles and complex depictions of characters with disabilities, both visible and invisible.
"Whenever awards season rolls around, we always hope to see a diverse group of projects that reflect all of us, in body and mind," hetold the BBC in 2021.
"Watching the awareness grow around disability representation has been great to see, but breakthroughs sometimes come in pieces and moments instead of larger change," he said.
Mitte's other on-screen credits include Hannah Montana, Switched at Birth, Westhampton and his latest project, Talking to Strangers, which came out earlier this year.
Additional reporting by Rebecka Pieder

title: UK growth upgraded but energy prices and rates to bite in 2027
summary: The IMF report comes as final preparations are being made to the first Budget under Prime Minister Andy Burham.
body:
The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit growth in 2027, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said.
The organisation's latest report, which is closely watched by the government, said the UK economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027.
Economies across the world have proved more resilient to the energy price shock caused by the US-Iran war, the IMF said, but it warned the economic fallout from the conflict remained "highly uncertain".
Chancellor John Healey said the government would look to "provide some breathing space" for households in the Budget.
Healey is making the final preparations to Andy Burnham's new-look government's tax and spending plans, which will be announced on 28 October.
Government borrowing costs have surged, placing pressure on the chancellor to ensure his plans are credible in the eyes of financial markets, which the UK relies on to borrow money.
But in its economic forecast, the IMF projected that the UK would have a sharp fall in borrowing and the lowest annual rate of borrowing of all G7 countries - the group of the world's most advanced economies - over the next five years.
The UK is estimated to have the lowest annual deficit - the difference between what the government spends and brings in through taxes in a year - by 2031, suggesting it thinks public spending will be cut in coming years.
The head of the IMF has previously called on the world's advanced economiesto cut borrowing and reduce debt levels.
The reversal of downgrades to economic forecasts made at the start of the US-Iran war, mean the UK is expected to have the second-fasted growing economy in the G7 along with Germany.
But growth is estimated to slow in 2027 to 1.2% due to higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weighing on household spending and business investment.
Healey acknowledged that wars in the Middle East and Europe were "hitting people in the UK and around the world", but added that "Britain's economy is showing strong international resilience".
When the economy is growing, businesses tend to invest more, more jobs are created and people, on average, tend to feel better off. The opposite can occur if the economy stagnates or shrinks.
Economists have suggested Healey faces having to find£35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget.
On Tuesday, the Resolution Foundation called on the chancellor to make "make repairs" to the public finances, but said well-targeted support was needed for those "struggling to heat their homes".
"The challenge of continuing to bring down borrowing must be paired with the pressing need for fresh cost of living support to help families facing a difficult winter ahead," the think tank said.
Andrew Griffith, Conservative shadow chancellor, said if Healey "reaches for more tax rises" in his Budget, "he is choosing slower growth and working people will pay for it".
Burnham has pledged to create "good growth in every postcode" as part of his plans to giving nations and regions more control, but hisstrategy has faced criticism inside his own party.
The IMF said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices, with inflation expected to average 3.3% this year and remain above the Bank of England's 2% target in 2027 at 2.8%.
The Bank itself has predicted inflation could rise above 4% at the beginning of next year - making it more likely that interest rates will rise.
Healey is expected to meet with other finance ministers at the IMF's annual meeting in Bangkok, Thailand, on Tuesday to discuss how the economic impact of the Middle East and European conflicts could be limited.
The IMF said the global economy had shown a "remarkable capacity to absorb shocks" not just from the current Middle East conflict, but also from the Covid pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

title: I earn £120,000 a year making social media videos go viral
summary: Social media "clippers" make short, vertical videos that appear on the likes of Instagram and TikTok.
body:
Eknoor Singh's successful social media video clips include one of popstar Dua Lipa
Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year.
The 22-year-old Londoner is a professional "clipper". He is paid by clients to make short, vertical videos for social media, in the hope of them going viral.
"The more views a clip gets, the more money I make," he says.
The way it typically works is that the client - who could be anyone from a clothing brand to a record label, movie studio, podcaster or influencer - has a longer video that the clipper watches first.
He or she then makes 30 to 60-second clips of what they consider to be the best bit or bits, and uploads them to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or other platforms.
The idea is that the clippers, who are typically aged from 16 to 25, will have a better understanding of what will connect with that demographic, and get the short videos as many views as possible.
With clippers able to earn up to $3 (£2.30) per 1,000 views across platforms, it can be very lucrative if a particular clip does take off.
Singh says he got hooked on clipping last year when he made $300 from posting a short video of popstar Dua Lipa on Instagram.
"I was like, 'OK, this is a lot of money for simply posting a video.' I instantly knew how lucrative it could be."
Now he says he is earning "at least £10,000 a month".
He adds that he looks for clips that are funny, quick to watch and engaging, such as a short video he made in May of Sabrina Carpenter's reaction to having the tails of her dress stepped on at the Met Gala in New York. Singh did not reveal who the client was.
Singh's clip of Sabrina Carpenter went viral
For 24-year-old clipper Ethan Weems from Wichita, Kansas, it's a lucrative side hustle to his other video-making work. He says he makes "at least $1,000 a month" from clipping.
He does this by making short videos for YouTuber and podcaster Caleb Hammer, who is best known for hosting a show called Financial Audit, which analyses the personal finances of his guests.
Weems says clipping helps him make a living from home – giving him more time to spend with his wife and one-year-old son. "I don't want that typical nine-to-five job where I have to go into an office every day," he says.
Yet while some clippers can make good money, social media consultant Lia Haberman cautions that there are very few of them. "It mirrors the creator economy more broadly. The vast majority make little to nothing," she says.
Meanwhile, streaming industry analyst Devin Nash says it's easy to underestimate the time required to make clipping a success. He warns that successful clippers must "watch hours and hours of content, and they just live in that world".
Ethan Weems says the income helps him continue to work from home
Connecting clippers with their prospective clients are a number of intermediary websites, where available video jobs are listed.
These range from pages on general online forums such as Reddit and Discord, to dedicated clipping sites such as Clipping Culture, Vyro, Whop and Kick.
The latter websites take a fee from the companies wanting the work done. Clipping Culture lists clients including Capital Records, Universal Music Group and HBO Max.
For firms such as these, hiring a teenager or 20-something working from his or her bedroom is far cheaper than paying for traditional adverts on social media, and likely to be more effective in terms of getting eyeballs.
That's the experience of Boxabl, a Las Vegas-based firm that makes modular homes. "I think we've done probably a billion views [of clips] so far," says founder Galiano Tiramani, who features in many of the company's videos.
In the UK, Jimmy McLoughlin, a former Downing Street adviser and now host of the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast, has also embraced clips.
"The clips are almost like trailers for the main events," he says. For instance, a recent podcast with Prime Minister Andy Burnham "had close to 50,000 long plays, but in terms of clips, it's done millions".
Eknoor Singh says he can make clips anywhere with just his mobile and a good internet connection
Evan Stanfield, the founder and boss of Clipping Culture, is himself just 21. He set up the business last year after dropping out of the University of Kansas.
Stanfield says that the website connects brands to more than 340,000 clippers from all over the world. He has a simple theory for the popularity of short videos: "People's attention spans are getting shorter and shorter."
He adds that making the clips is a young person's game because "they're most of the consumers of short-form videos".
Back in London, Eknoor Singh says he is "kind of clipping non-stop", wherever he is.
"I could be anywhere. I could go on holiday and make money."

title: Heating oil customers face tough winter despite shake-up promise
summary: Heating oil customers facing soaring bills are promised better regulation of the sector by the government.
body:
Heating oil customers facing soaring bills have been promised better regulation of the sector by the government.
Ministers say they will tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things go wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed.
With prices close to having doubled in the past year, some campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from the same cap as regular, variable gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales.
But there is no sign of the government proposing such a change, nor when the stricter rules will take effect.
Ministers said they would work with industry to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition".
In the meantime, oil users have been offered discounts on heat pumps, a code of practice is in place, and industry practices setting minimum order volumes at 500 litres for some consumers will be reviewed. Domestic tanks typically hold between 1,000 and 2,000 litres.
The government said this had left some people having to pay for more heating oil than they might need.
Buy now or wait and hope? Families face gamble on heating oil
Prices have soared since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran. In March, the government announceda support package worth £53mfor low-income families who use heating oil.
The funding is distributed by local authorities, which set their own criteria for eligibility.
A subsequent inquiry by the UK's competition watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority, found that 1,700 households were forced to "re-order at significantly higher prices or go without fuel" after the war broke out, costing them up to £350.
But those whose orders were cancelled and prices raised were told they were entitled to compensation.
The government has now announced it will accept the CMA's recommendation to strengthen regulation in the sector.
Energy minister Polly Billington said: "Thousands of heating oil customers felt they had nowhere to turn when they paid the price of rising oil and gas costs earlier this year.
"We won't accept that. Energy is an essential good and people should not have to think twice about whether they're protected in the market. That's why we will reform the sector."
Nick, a heating oil customer from West Suffolk, told the BBC's Your Voice that "off-grid households remain a major policy blind spot" for the government.
"Any protection from UK government for domestic heating oil users will be very welcome, providing this is for all domestic heating oil users," the 28-year-old said.
He rents a three-bedroom home with his partner. He said they had seen prices more than double in a year, to quotes of 111p per litre.
"Heating my home is now no longer another household bill, but almost an investment," he said.
He called on tax cuts for customers, or the extension of the price cap to heating oil - a demand also made by charity National Energy Action.
Tim Buckman, chief executive of price comparison site Boiler Juice, told the BBC he wants stronger protections for consumers but the main problem was that heating oil is twice as expensive as it was before the war.
"Just putting regulation in place is not going to reduce the price for customers. What we would like to see is the VAT off heating oil or targeting that specifically."
Some 1.5 million households depend on heating oil, but they do not have the same consumer protections as electricity and gas customers.
However, energy regulator Ofgem, which sets the cap for standard variable tariffs, only covers England, Wales and Scotland.
Most heating oil customers are in Northern Ireland, where 60% of households rely on it, but where regulation is separate.
It is likely Ofgem will regulate heating oil in England, Scotland and Wales, and the UK government said it would "engage with the Northern Ireland Executive as they consider these recommendations in parallel".

title: Bumble shares soar after report dating firm in $1bn takeover talks
summary: The jump pushed Bumble's stock market valuation to more than $580m but that is still far below their peak of more than $14bn.
body:
Bumble founder Whitney Wolfe Herd
Shares in dating app company Bumble soared by almost 50% on Monday after a report that it is in advanced talks to be bought for around $1bn (£757m).
Technology holding company Ithaca could announce a deal to buy the Texas-based firm as early as this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.
The jump in Bumble's shares pushed its stock market valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached afterlisting on the Nasdaq in 2021.
Bumble is one of the world's most downloaded dating apps, operating in a crowded market where growth has slowed. The BBC has contacted Bumble and Ithaca for comment.
Bumble was launched in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, who was also a co-founder of dating app giant Tinder.
Wolfe Herd built Bumble's brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches.
Itrecently abandoned that rule, prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals.
"Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August.
Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates.
Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating.
Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services.
Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021.
According a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier.
Some single people are insteadturning to board game get-togethers, book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner.

title: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?
summary: Meeting travellers' expectations could be challenging, experts warn.
body:
The early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt.
Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night.
This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers.
Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after.
Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working.
Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership.
August's 90-second power outage sparked chaos for rail commuters
But in reality, plans are still in their early stages. Big structural changes have yet to be introduced. And experts caution that it's too early to say how successful these will be.
So can rail nationalisation meet the public's expectations? Or are the ongoing delays and cancellations that we're currently seeing under a part-nationalised network a sign that it might struggle to deliver real improvement?
South Western Railway (SWR) was nationalised in May 2025, the first of six services to be brought into public ownership under Labour so far.
At Woking station, which is served by SWR, regular commuter Leo tells me he had been optimistic about public ownership, but hasn't noticed it making any difference so far: "I think the phrase 'emperor's new clothes' comes to mind… it's still unreliable."
SWR saw a clear increase in cancellations during its first year in public hands.
But how much of this was due to nationalisation?
The Conservatives have cited SWR as an example of how public control does not necessarily mean improvements or fix key problems.
But the government argues SWR's early period in public hands was affected by high summer temperatures, signal failures and trespass incidents.
Lord Hendy, the rail minister, says work to turn the operator around has included introducing long-delayed new trains on suburban routes and recruiting more drivers, resulting in a drop in those cancellations that are due to staff shortages.
TransPennine Express was nationalised in May 2023, under the Conservative government. Many passengers had been at their wits' end as the operator struggled to fulfil its timetable and suffered from poor industrial relations.
A plan to improve reliability was put in place, which included cutting some services and even removing one type of train as a way of sorting out staffing problems. A new deal with the drivers' union also helped - something an insider at the former private sector operator claimed to me their company had not been permitted to do.
So has it worked? Cancellations have fallen noticeably. But they were still above the Great Britain average in the year to August.
It's really important to say the data can only tell us so much. There are so many different factors that might affect the performance of each service: for example, the state of the infrastructure it relies on, weather events or simply how well it was working before the government took over.
Plus, of the operators nationalised since Labour came to power, only SWR and c2c have completed a whole year in public hands. Even for those nationalised years earlier, the picture is clouded by the impact of the pandemic, when passenger numbers fell off a cliff.
But according to Alex Hynes, chief executive of DfT Operator Limited (DfTO), the government company that currently owns publicly-run operators, it has been possible to make some short-term changes. Notably, these include making one team jointly responsible for managing infrastructure and passenger train services in some areas including the south-west of England.
"The railway is a system: track, train, people," he says. "So by putting one person in charge, they can fix all elements of the system to deliver a better service to customers."
Hynes also gives examples of changes on the recently nationalised Thameslink; investment in better cleaning, improving toilets and replacing unpopular upright "ironing-board" seats.
But when it comes to the pure performance data of operators nationalised in the past few years - delays, cancellations -  can we really draw any conclusions yet to tell us whether the policy is working?
"I think it's completely hopeless to try and do that assessment over such a short period," Stephen Glaister, a former chair of regulator the Office of Rail and Road who is now emeritus professor of transport and infrastructure at Imperial College London. He thinks a decade is needed to assess the impact of nationalisation.
The government argues that official data suggests publicly owned train operators are performing better on punctuality and cancellations overall than those still under DfT contracts to private operators.
Experts point out that whoever is running the passenger trains, some limitations remain. Many delays happen because infrastructure, like signals, fails. There's only so much capacity on the existing network. And getting better trains or more staff can take years.
The view that privatisation ultimately failed, leaving unreliable services and high fares, may be widespread. However, Prof Glaister argues that for a few years in the 1990s, the old privatised system actually worked well. Operating costs and subsidies were falling while the number of train services and passengers went up, he says.
And in the current context, it's important to be clear about what nationalisation really means.
The railways Labour inherited weren't, in truth, completely privatised, and nationalisation doesn't mean a return to British Rail.
For example, the infrastructure manager Network Rail has been fully under public control for over two decades. A number of train companies including LNER and Northern had already been nationalised under the Conservatives. Scotrail, Transport for Wales and Caledonian Sleeper are controlled by devolved national governments.
And even those operators still on contracts issued by the DfT at Westminster have been heavily controlled by the government for years. During Covid, private operators started being paid a fixed fee to run services, while the taxpayer took on the financial risk. The terms of the contracts meant train companies had to "ask government for permission to blow their nose", according to one senior industry executive, who asked not to be named so they could speak freely.
Highly profitable rolling stock companies ("ROSCOS") still own the actual trains. Freight companies operate privately too, and there are a handful of fully commercial "open access operators" on the rails like Lumo, Hull Trains and Grand Central - although there are concerns within the industry that these could end up squeezed.
So what is often referred to as the nationalisation of the railways, in fact amounts to gradually returning passenger train operators run by private companies to public hands as their contracts expire - and making this the default.
This is not all that's happening, though. The government hopes that re-organising the railways under a new publicly run body, Great British Railways (GBR), will make a big difference. This will bring together the running of trains and tracks, ending the current fragmented system.
A botched rail timetable introduction in 2018 was the spark for the then-Conservative government to eventually propose GBR as a new overarching body - although the Tories believe private competition should not be excluded from the system.
Some trains are already covered in distinctive GBR branding, but the organisation still doesn't exist. A new law to create it is making its way through parliament. Unknowns remain, like exactly how GBR will interact with devolved governments, and who its senior leaders will be.
GBR's livery has already been unveiled
Transport expert and author Prof Jon Shaw, of the University of Plymouth, says the idea of a "single guiding mind" should create "a better planned railway that's more aligned to the customer".
Prof Shaw thinks potential benefits include better long-term planning around rolling-stock and timetables, and the removal of "the compensation merry-go-round", where train companies and Network Rail argue about whose fault a delay was.
Hynes says: "The way you get the railway to work is you get the infrastructure and the trains and the people working in harmony because it's a system. And we can do that in a publicly owned GBR railway in a way that we haven't been able to do for a generation."
But Prof Shaw cautions of potential pitfalls. For example, "there remains very little money", and "a massive issue is whether or not the rail minister or DfT more generally - or the Treasury - will be able to butt out" and leave rail leaders to run the railway.
Prof Glaister also fears politically sensitive aspects such as fares and levels of service could lead to politicians trying to run the railways themselves, because of the amount of public money involved.
"Actually, governments are not very good at running railways," he says. "So you want management who are somewhat independent and able to run it."
Lord Hendy insists that despite the Transport Secretary having ultimate sign-off on GBR's strategy, the body will be genuinely arms-length from government.

title: Burnham to push for new post-Brexit deals at EU summit
summary: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister was "unpicking" the deal the UK signed with the EU.
body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told MPs he will push for new post-Brexit deals with the EU at a summit next month.
He said "deeper cooperation" on some key issues - including youth mobility, food and drink, and energy - would help drive economic growth in the UK.
In a statement to MPs, Burnham also warned the EU'sMade In Europe plansposed "a risk to UK manufacturing" and said he was in talks to get "an arrangement" that worked for the UK. The EU proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors but could impact British industry and supply chains.
But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister was "unpicking" the deal the UK signed with the EU.
Although he said he was keen to negotiate a closer relationship with the EU, Burnham made clear Labour's manifesto commitments not to return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement, would stay in place until the next election.
Burnham said the "immediate priority" was securing a successful outcome at the November summit, adding: "I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.
"At every stage, the British public will be the boss, and I am clear that public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach like the one I am suggesting."
While the prime minister has committed to the current Labour manifesto's red lines about Brexit, in interviews after Labour conference, he did not rule out a new manifesto, which could include re-joining the EU.
It is increasingly clear that economic growth, and cooperation on illegal immigration, are going to be at the centre of No 10's arguments when it comes to selling a closer relationship both at - and beyond - next month's summit.
The Brexit withdrawal agreement in 2020 agreed the UK's "divorce bill" payments to the EU, and allowed the rules and regulations in the UK to start to diverge from those in the EU, which was necessary in order tonegotiate trade deal with other countries.
But the divergence in food standards caused problems for UK food exports to its largest market, a problem that Sir Keir Starmer started to try to fix by renegotiating some common rules to reduce red tape.
In May 2025, this resulted in a post-Brexit deal agreeing continued access to UK waters for EU fishing boats until 2038, in return for a deal to reduce checks on food exports to the EU, which meant the UK was able to sell raw burgers and sausages back into the EU for the first time since Brexit.
The summit next month will see a series of deals with the EU on the table, Burnham told MPs, including food and drink, energy trading, and coordinating on immigration.
Burnham claimed these agreements could add the equivalent of £10bn per year to the economy by 2040, arguing that it would be a "dereliction of duty" to turn away from the chance to cut bureaucracy.
"At present entire truckloads of plants or fresh produce can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or a minor paperwork delay," he said.
"Fresh meat and fish spoil while waiting in trucks, and tonnes of exports have to be written off. Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around £100m in lost exports.
"British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU, seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned - this is having a real impact on businesses and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage."
The prime minister said a fresh agreement at the EU summit would also "ease the pressure on prices in the supermarket".
He said securing an energy deal, involving emissions trading, could "lower energy costs for households and businesses alike", adding this could cut wholesale energy costs by 20% in Northern Ireland.
Burnham said he also hoped to rebuild links with EU police and security agencies to boost information-sharing and help tackle smuggling gangs.
And he said being open about a new relationship with the EU was necessary to get a good deal on all these things: "If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have.
"Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain."

The Conservative leader criticised the prime minister for "unpicking the deal this country signed with the EU a decade after the referendum".
Badenoch added Burnham would not get a better deal than the one secured by the Conservatives, accusing him of giving the game away ahead of the summit.
"His exact words earlier this year were, 'the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments' and yet here he is unpicking the deal this country signed with the EU a decade after the referendum," she said.
"He is not going to get a better deal. The EU are tough negotiators, and it's not just that the EU are tough negotiators, he has already revealed his entire negotiating hand.
"He has just blurted out everything he wants in this statement and I will tell him now, as a former trade secretary, this is not how you conduct negotiations."
Mocking the previous negotiations, Burnham said: "She says that, oh, I've revealed what I want to do and this isn't any way to negotiate it - because the Tories were so good, weren't they, at negotiating deals with our partners?"
Conservative Nigel Huddleston pointed out that post-Brexit trade deals with countries like the US and India meant a new EU deal would not be straightforward.
He said: "As a former trade minister can I also advise the PM, because his officials and minsters clearly have not, that actually it may not be as easy after all, because of clauses in some of the 70-something other trade deals that we did with other countries, to unwind all the things he would like to do."
However, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey welcomed Burnham's recognition of  the "damage" of Brexit and called on him to go further, dropping Labour's red lines and opening negotiations on joining the EU single market and customs union.
