title: Government expands police support to political figures who are not MPs
summary: Shabana Mahmood says there is "insufficient protection" for those who play a role in public life.
body:
Political figures who are not currently MPs will be given police support, the home secretary has announced.
Shabana Mahmood told MPs there was "insufficient protection" for those serving in public life and that the new announcement will cover peers, former MPs and party spokespeople.
She also announced an urgent, independent review of security arrangements for high-profile figures including politicians and royals.
It comes three months after Reform UK spokeswoman and former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her home in Devon,having been hit on the head with a hammer 21 times as she ate lunch.
Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with her murder, and he was alsocharged with preparing acts of terroragainst Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.
Kerry is alleged to havecarried out research on prominent targetsover a period of two years, including trying to gain entry into Farage's London home.
Speaking in the Commons on Monday, Mahmood said that "robustdebate and criticism are part of this job - threats, abuse and violence are not."
She did not elaborate on what the support would involve, but told MPs it would include access to a named police officer and help with wider security measures.
The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years, following the murders of Conservative MP Sir David Amess in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox in 2016.
"We owe it to them and to everyone who believes in a fair and open country to ensure that those who serve at all levels receive the protection they deserve," Mahmood added.
The "root and branch" independent review into security arrangements will be led by former national security advisor Stephen Lovegrove, and will look into "physical threats, online risks and the dangers posed within our more polarised society".
Mahmood confirmed that the review will report within six months, and build on the existing work of Sir Robert Buckland, who is leading a separate review into the murder of Sir David.
In response, shadow home secretary Chris Philp welcomed the extension of protective measures, saying threats to elected representatives are threats to democracy.
Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf welcomed the review, but added: "It is disappointing that it took the murder of one of our colleagues, countless threats towards our party spokespeople and months of campaigning from Reform UK to make this government take action."
Reform hasin recent months accusedthe government of a "dereliction of duty" over Farage's taxpayer-funded security, claiming it had previously been "downgraded" - a charge that the Home Office has said is "categorically untrue".
Decisions over the security of current MPs and members of the House of Lords are made by the House of Parliament's security team.
There is a separate, independent committee, the Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec), to deal with high-profile political candidates, which is staffed by officials from the Home Office, the Cabinet Office, and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.
The Jo Cox Foundation welcomed the home secretary's announcement but said "strengthening physical security" alone was not enough.
"We must also tackle the root causes - including online harms and education - to prevent future attacks," its chief executive Olivia Field said in a statement on X.
According todata released to the BBC in April, the number of alleged offences against MPs have increased year-on-year, with 976 recorded in 2025, compared to 364 in 2019.
MPs reported 4,064 crimes to the Met's Parliamentary Liaison Team between 2019 and 2025. Most offences were related to malicious communications followed by harassment, and criminal damage to a building.
In 2025, there were 50 death threats reported - up from 31 the previous year.

title: It is inconceivable to think Russia did not try to interfere in Brexit vote, says PM
summary: Andy Burnham says he is not questioning the legitimacy of the 2016 vote after facing questions from MPs.
body:
Andy Burnham has said it is "inconceivable" to think that Russia did not try to interfere in the 2016 EU referendum.
The prime minister told MPs he had not been questioning the legitimacy of the Brexit vote when he told the Rest is Politics podcast that it was "clear" there had been interference by Moscow.
His comments to the podcast provoked angry responses from some Brexit campaigners, with Reform UK leader Nigel Farage calling the prime minister "a liar".
A No 10 spokesperson said that while the prime minister believed it was highly likely Russia tried to influence the referendum result, he did not believe those efforts were successful.
In an interview, released on Monday, Burnham toldThe Rest is Politics podcast,,externalthat upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there had been Russian interference in the vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was."
He added: "I think we've been too much on the back foot on that actually and we haven't informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas."
Burnham did not provide details about the extent or nature of Russian activities in the referendum during the interview and when pressed on the subject in the House of Commons on Monday afternoon appeared to be less definitive.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister had "implied that the referendum result was illegitimate because of Russian interference".
She asked the prime minister to confirm that he believed the referendum was legitimate adding: "If not, will he publish the evidence that Russia swung the result of the 2016 referendum."
Burnham said he had "implied no such thing" but added that it was a "matter of record" that Russiasought to interfere in the 2019 general election.
"We think it is inconceivable that this was the first time," he said.
Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey welcomed Burnham's comments, saying it "took courage after the Conservatives took so long suppressing the evidence".
He also urged the prime minister to publish evidence of interference in the Brexit referendum as well as other UK votes.
Burnham did not commit to making public any evidence but said he wanted to ensure that the British democratic system was protected in the future.

Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation?
Responding to Burnham's initial comments earlier in the day, Farage said: "The prime minister is a liar, yes, a liar."
"There was no Russian interference - the Russian hoax has run all the way through this," he added.
"This is out-of-touch, out-of-date Andy Burnham with all sorts of bizarre ideas."
Former prime minister Boris Johnson wrote on X that in 2016, when he became foreign secretary the security services had told him "there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".
He added: "Either the security services have changed their view - which would be very odd - or Burnham is lying about what he has been told."
In 2020,a parliamentary reportdid not reach a firm conclusion on whether Russia had tried to intervene in UK elections and referendums, but criticised the government for failing to fully assess and counter the threat from Russian 'troll' accounts on social media.
Asked in 2017, if he had seen evidence of Russia successfully meddling in UK elections,Johnson, who was then-foreign secretary said:"Nyet [Russian for no], not a sausage."
Earlier this year, the governmentpublished an independent review,externalon foreign influence in UK politics which said there were attempts to "sow distrust and exacerbate divisions in UK society with the ultimate aim of undermining confidence in our democracy".
Report author Philip Rycroft said it was difficult to establish the impact of these efforts and that the public "can be credited with sufficient common sense to see of the more egregious attempts to suborn their opinions".
However, he added that while there was no "immediate crisis" in British democracy "there is no guarantee that this will persist".

title: Reform pledges to suspend UK's asylum system for up to five years
summary: All asylum applications would be rejected and existing ones voided, with all claimants marked for deportation.
body:
Nigel Farage unveiled the plans in Hythe, Kent on Monday lunchtime
Reform UK has announced plans to effectively close down the UK's asylum system for a full parliamentary term if elected.
The party said all new asylum applications would be rejected and existing applications voided, with all claimants marked for deportation. It said no grants of humanitarian protection or refugee status would be made, while legal refugee routes and resettlement schemes would end.
Reform said it would also scrap the asylum tribunal system and deport 90,000 people currently with appeal cases, with home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf saying "Britain is full".
Labour called the proposals a "clear sign of desperation and weakness" and the Refugee Council branded them "unworkable".
Reform said its existing plans to make migrants who have entered the UK illegally, overstayed a visa or originated from a safe country ineligible for asylum would effectively prevent any current asylum claimant "from ever having their case heard".
The party said it would therefore "suspend the asylum system entirely for a full parliamentary term".
A parliamentary term usually lasts five years unless an early UK general election is called.
Under further proposals, Reform said it would pull the UK out of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), repeal the Human Rights Act 1998 and disapply the 1951 Refugee Convention to prevent legal challenges to its plans.
The party said it would ban British visas for countries such as Pakistan, Somalia, Eritrea, Syria, Afghanistan and Sudan if they refuse to allow deportation flights to land in their country.
Nigel Farage and Zia Yusuf gave speeches in front of a replica "mega dinghy" involved in Channel crossings - which Farage said showed it was no longer "a small boats crisis"
For countries without a significant legal foreign national presence in the UK, the party said it would consider asset freezes and potential tariffs on goods and services for non-compliance.
Announcing the plans in a speech in Hythe, Kent on Monday, party leader Nigel Farage said the UK is "now living in a national security emergency".
"We want to get back to being a normal country, a country that puts national security at the top of the agenda, a country that does everything it can to protect its citizens."
He claimed the plans were "going to save us a fortune" but declined to say how many civil servants would be required to process the deportations, other than that Home Office staff currently overseeing asylum claims would be reprioritised.
In a speech, Yusuf said he would "have to embark on the biggest mass deportation programme this country has ever seen" if made home secretary but "we will not be returning people to harm".
"We've got to prioritise the British people," Yusuf said, pointing to Britons facing long waits for emergency care and people in their 30s and 40s having to live at home because of rent prices.
He claimed themillions of unauthorised immigrants deportedunder former US President Barack Obama's administration showed there was "precedent" for the party's plans.
Reform also said it would create a specialised agency focusing on the detention and deportation of those in the UK illegally, with 24,000 to 28,000 detention spaces needed - but is unclear how this would provide enough capacity.
Between 1 January and 5 October 2026, a total of 20,478 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 40% on the same period the previous year.
These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.
Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.
Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.
Boats that arrived in the UK from 6 October 2025 to 5 October 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.
Experts sayovercrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).
When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.
The government has pledged to“smash the gangs”behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.
People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026.
In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.
Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year.
There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.
The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.
Previous pledges from Reform include a review of all asylum claims from the last five years and returning all small boat arrivals.
In response to the latest announcement, Jon Featonby, chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said "closing our asylum system would cause chaos".
"Desperate people would still arrive on our shores, but instead of entering an orderly system, they would be driven underground and vulnerable to exploitation and abuse," he told the BBC.
All the main political parties should focus on speeding up asylum decisions "so that instead of languishing in accommodation paid for by the taxpayer, those found to be refugees can move into proper housing, start work or training, and begin contributing to their communities, while those with no right to stay can be helped to return with dignity," he added.
Bridget Phillipson said Farage was "casting around for more and more extreme policies" ashe deals with questions about financesand rival party Restore Britain.
The Labour chair said her party is showing "we can control immigration and get numbers down with serious action, not by abandoning the asylum system altogether", adding the "right approach" is "not giving up or caving to the most extreme voices, but ensuring that the rules we have are properly enforced".
In March, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said any asylum seeker given refugee status will now only be offered temporary protection, reviewed every 30 months.
In September, she also reopened a scheme to resettle refugees in the UK, saying she hoped that offering "safe and legal" routes would deter small boat crossings.
Reform has questioned if safe routes for Afghans and Palestinians to the UK should stay, but said it would keep a temporary settlement scheme for Ukrainians fleeing the war against Russia, as well asEU settled status with benefit cuts.
Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the proposals "largely copy" his party's policies, arguing: "Only the Conservatives have a serious and credible plan to fix our borders."
The Tories previously said they would task officials with removing 750,000 illegal immigrants within five years, under Trump-style deportation plans.
Lib Dems home affairs spokesperson Max Wilkinson said the "UK can only restore order, control and fairness by joining the EU migration and asylum pact", which increases the number of irregular migrants returned to their home countries and spreads responsibility for asylum seekers across the EU.

title: Britain won't tolerate threats on our soil, Miliband says as he summons Iran ambassador
summary: The prime minister says Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard "almost certainly" directed the RAF Fairford incident.
body:
A large cordon was put in place around the base and dozens of homes were evacuated
The foreign secretary has summoned the Iranian ambassador to make clear that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil" following last month's incident at RAF Fairford.
Ed Miliband said attempts by Iran to undermine the UK's security "through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs the incident in Gloucestershire was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard", while the home secretary said the likely coordinator was a "known individual based in Iran".
Iran's ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, said Tehran was not involved and was willing to cooperate with British authorities.
The Foreign Office has also sanctioned two Iranians, including the head of the regime's counterespionage operations - with both men subjected to travel bans and asset freezes.
Burnham also indicated Iran could be hit with further sanctions over its suspected role.
It comes as the UK and 28 other countries - including the US, Canada, Australia, France and Germany - issued a joint statement condemning "in the strongest terms" violent attacks by Iran.
The statement accuses Tehran of carrying out "lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities" and also recognises the UK's attribution of Iranian involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.
A huge police operation began after officers were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base in the early hours of 27 September.
Dozens of homes were evacuated in the nearby village of Whelford and a large cordon was put in place around the site.
So far, a total of seven men - all in their 20s - have been arrested and later bailed in connection with the incident. No one has been charged.
Last week, Downing Streetinsisted the airbase was safeafter the US withdrew all of its bombers – about a dozen B-1s from the base – back to their home stations on American soil.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved an American request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
A US state department spokesman confirmed that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had a call with Miliband on Monday where they discussed "holding Iran to account for its actions and of continued collaboration to secure US assets in the United Kingdom".
